To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the risk of developing distant metastases is reduced in patients who receive adjuvant radiation therapy (ART), and 2) the risk of dying from prostate cancer (overall survival) is not significantly improved with ART.

the use of ad-juvant radiotherapy after radical prostatectomy is associated with a reduction in PSA failure-free survival, a reduction in time-to-distant metastasis and a prolongation in overall sur-vival.

the SWOG study is the only RCT with a statistically significant reduction in time to metastasis and overall survival, and that the followup schedule may be a critical factor in the interpretation of the results of these studies.

the data support the use of ART for men who have pT3 disease or positive margins.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of metastasis and death from prostate cancer is reduced with the use of radiation therapy after surgery, regardless of whether it is given as an adjuvant or a salvage treatment.
we have a better understanding of what the optimal timing is to initiate therapy in patients who are at high risk for recurrence.
we have to be careful in interpreting the results of these trials, especially the SWOG study which is the only one to date to demonstrate a survival advantage.
